item.title: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
item.description:
North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
South Korea says North Korea has launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the seaByHYUNG-JIN KIM Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 11:48 PM
Share
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters Thursday, South Korea’s military said, days after the North threatened to resume front-line propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy new weapons along the rivals’ tense border.
The launches also followed leader Kim Jong Un’s surprise weekend visit to China, the North's main ally and economic pipeline, to push for greater cooperation.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected about 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the North's eastern costal town of Wonsan and that they each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles). It said South Korea's military maintained its readiness to repel any provocations by North Korea under a solid alliance with the United States.
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected ballistic missile launch by North Korea.
Animosity between the Koreas have deepened since last month’s land mine blasts at the border that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of planting mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded it apologize. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea said it would restart propaganda broadcasts and place new weapons systems on alert along the border in protest of what it called repeated warning shots by South Korean troops at border areas. South Korea later proposed talks on clarifying the border to prevent accidental clashes, but North Korea hasn't responded.

item.title: After years under fire, a rare quiet settles over Ukrainian city as truce holds
item.description:
After years under fire, a rare quiet settles over Ukrainian city as truce holds
A planned six-day ceasefire brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump has brought rare quiet to the Ukrainian-held city of KhersonByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 1:41 PM
KHERSON, Ukraine -- A planned six-day ceasefire brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump and tied to a humanitarian aid mission in a Russian-occupied town has brought rare quiet to the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson across the water.
Four years ago, crowds filled the central square of this southern port city, draped in Ukrainian flags and hugging the troops who had ended months of Russian occupation. Many thought the hardest part was behind them. Instead, the war took a new form.
Kherson sits directly across the Dnipro River from the Russian-occupied part of the region. From the other bank, Moscow forces have kept up regular attacks with everything from guided aerial bombs to explosive-laden first-person-view drones that prowl the skies, turning the city into a front line.
Melania Trump, who previously hasn't been publicly involved in ceasefire negotiations, brokered the localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city that she said is “on the brink of disaster.” It spread to the other side of the river within the Kherson region, which is only partially under Russian control.
A local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. Tuesday to allow medicine, food and water to be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened later in the week. The situation in Oleshky is desperate, with food and medical supplies running perilously low for the up to 2,000 people still there, as drones and land mines restrict movement.

item.title: UN reports a sharp rise in Afghanistan poppy cultivation despite a Taliban ban
item.description:
UN reports a sharp rise in Afghanistan poppy cultivation despite a Taliban ban
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reports a sharp rise in poppy cultivation and opium production in Afghanistan over the past yearByThe Associated PressOctober 29, 2026, 3:56 AM
Share
KABUL, Afghanistan -- Poppy cultivation and opium production in Afghanistan rose sharply over the past year, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said on Thursday, describing it as the first significant increase since the country’s Taliban rulers imposed a narcotics ban in 2022.
The agency attributed the rise to deepening poverty, which it said has driven some farmers to cultivate opium clandestinely. It called on the international community to provide greater support to farmers to help curb reliance on illicit crops.
Afghanistan was the world’s biggest opium producer and a major source of heroin in Europe and Asia when the Taliban seized power in August 2021. They pledged to wipe out the country’s drug cultivation industry and imposed a formal ban in April 2022, dealing a heavy blow to hundreds of thousands of farmers and day laborers who relied on proceeds from the crop to survive.
The U.N. agency said cultivation was up 330% and production rose by 400% compared to last year. Cultivation rose to more than 43,000 hectares (106,000 acres) in 2026 from 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) a year earlier, it said.
Farmers were concealing small poppy plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds to evade detection, the report said.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” a statement quoted the agency’s executive director, Monica Juma, as saying.

item.title: Oxygen cylinder explodes inside ambulance, killing at least 10 in Pakistan
item.description:
Oxygen cylinder explodes inside ambulance, killing at least 10 in Pakistan
Officials say an oxygen cylinder exploded inside a parked ambulance at a government-run medical facility in southern Pakistan, killing at least 10 people, including a patient of the facilityByThe Associated PressOctober 29, 2026, 3:49 AM
KARACHI, Pakistan -- KARACHI, Pakistan (AP) — An oxygen cylinder exploded inside a parked ambulance at a government-run medical facility in southern Pakistan, killing at least 10 people, including a patient of the facility, police and hospital officials said Thursday.
The blast occurred overnight in Tharparkar district in the Sindh province, said district Police Chief Arif Aziz.
He said the victims included staff at the medical facility, patients, and their relatives.
Local police official Khalil Abro said patients were being transferred to another hospital when the explosion occurred. Images on social media and on television stations showed flames engulfing a vehicle, with one door open. Another image showed its blackened frame outside a building as people stood nearby.

item.title: Spain’s 4 deadly train crashes this year, at a glance
item.description:
Spain’s 4 deadly train crashes this year, at a glance
Wednesday’s collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain was the second fatal crash in nine months on a network long held up as a national success storyByTHOMAS ADAMSON Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 10:56 AM
Share
PARIS -- Wednesday’s deadly collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain was the second fatal crash in nine months on a network that has long been a source of national pride.
Spain has spent decades building Europe’s largest high-speed rail network, second only to China’s.
Until this year, there had been no fatal incidents on its dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992, officials said.
That ended with the disaster near Adamuz, which killed 46 people in January.
That crash and Wednesday's both involved trains run by the state-owned company RENFE and private company IRYO on the track linking Madrid with the Andalusia region.
The year has also seen fatal incidents on a commuter line near Barcelona and at a railroad crossing in central Spain.
A look at four fatal train incidents in Spain this year:
Two high-speed trains, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, collided near Urda, in Toledo province, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, regional authorities said.
One train struck the rear of another that had stopped, derailing two cars. The crash halted high-speed services between Madrid and Andalusia.
An Iryo train traveling from Malaga to Madrid derailed near Adamuz, in southern Spain, and collided with an oncoming Renfe train heading to Huelva.
Forty-six people were killed and more than 100 injured. The impact sent the Renfe train’s first two cars down an embankment.

item.title: Houthis say Saudi-led airstrikes killed 14 at a market in northern Yemen, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Houthis say Saudi-led airstrikes killed 14 at a market in northern Yemen, and other Mideast news
Iran-backed Houthi rebels say Saudi-led airstrikes have killed 14 people in a busy market in northern YemenByThe Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 7:14 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
Iran-backed Houthi rebels say Saudi-led airstrikes have killed 14 people in a busy market in northern Yemen.
Yemeni officials, meanwhile, appealed for international support to protect civilians in Taiz as the Houthis tightened their siege of the city.
Separately, a police officer guarding the Israeli Embassy in the Serbian capital of Belgrade shot and killed a man who attacked him with a knife. Police said the incident was a “terrorist attack.”
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here.
Saudi-led airstrikes hit a crowded market in northern Yemen on Wednesday, killing 14 people and wounding 15 others, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry. Three women were among the wounded, it said, adding that shops and houses nearby were heavily damaged.
The market near a gas station in al-Hazm, the capital of al-Jawf province, was packed with shoppers when the strikes hit, the ministry said in a statement. The ministry called the attack a war crime that requires an international investigation. There was no immediate statement from the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
An Associated Press reporter in the southern city of Aden witnessed explosions that shattered windows at the airport building and nearby homes after Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree urged everyone at the airport to evacuate.
Saree said a Saudi military cargo plane carrying weapons was there, without providing evidence.

item.title: Cyclone Arnab hits India's Andhra Pradesh state as tens of thousands evacuate
item.description:
Cyclone Arnab hits India's Andhra Pradesh state as tens of thousands evacuate
Officials say Cyclone Arnab crossed India’s Andhra Pradesh coast early Wednesday, a day after tens of thousands of people were forced to evacuate from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern stateByOMER FAROOQ Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 11:58 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
HYDERABAD, India -- Cyclone Arnab crossed India 's Andhra Pradesh coast in the early hours of Wednesday, officials said, a day after tens of thousands of people were evacuated from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state.
Prakhar Jain, head of the state���s disaster management authority, said the cyclone had weakened slightly before landfall but brought heavy to very heavy rainfall to several coastal districts, triggering widespread disruption in affected areas.
State disaster management officials said late Wednesday morning that wind speeds were up to 135 kph (84 mph).
Officials said the cyclone was expected to weaken further as it moved inland, with wind speeds likely to ease later in the day.
There were no immediate reports of casualties, but some damage was observed.
The India Meteorological Department said the landfall process was complete and heavy rainfall as well as strong winds would continue under the cyclone's influence in coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh and parts of southern Odisha state.
Cyclone Arnab weakened to a "severe" cyclonic storm Wednesday, IMD said in an update.

item.title: US and Japan agree to establish missile-production facility
item.description:
US and Japan agree to establish missile-production facility
The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief saidByJIM GOMEZ Associated Press and JOEAL CALUPITAN Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 8:02 PM
Share
CEBU, Philippines -- The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said late Wednesday. It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China’s growing aggression in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called “Operation Supercharge" are “essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, without elaborating or providing other details of the agreement. The U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets are one of the world’s most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he “shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before.”
“We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means...

item.title: French prosecutor seeks pretrial detention for suspect in shooting near Paris
item.description:
French prosecutor seeks pretrial detention for suspect in shooting near Paris
France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor has asked for a 39-year-old suspect to be held in pretrial detention over a suspected racist attack in the Paris suburbsBySYLVIE CORBET Associated PressOctober 29, 2026, 7:55 AM
PARIS -- France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor asked Thursday that a 39-year-old suspect be held in pretrial detention over a shooting in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded seven others, saying he targeted people he believed to be Muslim or from Africa.
The suspect, a 39-year-old French national identified by authorities as Kevin T., was arrested less than 20 minutes after the shooting began Friday in Trappes and neighboring La Verrière, a suburban area west of Paris. His last name has not been made public.
An 11-year-old girl was among the injured when a gunman fired from his vehicle at several locations along a 12-kilometer (7.5-mile) route.
The suspect “now acknowledged that the acts were premeditated,” national counterterrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen said. The suspect admitted to “specifically targeting” people he believed to be Muslim or from sub-Saharan Africa or North Africa based on their appearance, Christen said.
Christen added that the suspect said he chose the suburb of Trappes because it is “a haven for Islamists.”
He denied any terrorist intent and said “he had no regrets,” Christen added.
A judicial investigation has been opened into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the crimes were committed because of the victims’ actual or perceived race, ethnicity, nationality or religion.

item.title: Chileans push to protect oceans that have been hurt by intensive salmon farming
item.description:
Chileans push to protect oceans that have been hurt by intensive salmon farming
The remote Guaitecas Archipelago has more than 40 small islands and is a gateway to Chile’s Patagonia regionByELENA BASSO Associated PressOctober 28, 2026, 9:36 AM
Share
MELINKA, Chile -- Yesica Fabiana Leviñanco steers her small wooden boat while her partner, Paulo Vera Perez, dives into the cold ocean waters off the coast of southern Chile.
Within a few hours the couple, both in their mid-40s, has filled the boat with shellfish, sea urchins, mussels and crabs that Leviñanco will sell at the market in Melinka, the main island in the Guaitecas Archipelago.
Even a few years ago, such a haul would have been unthinkable.
“It seems incredible looking at it today, but for years the sea throughout this area was dead,” said Leviñanco. “There were no birds, fish or marine animals. A salmon-farming facility had destroyed everything.”
__
EDITORS' NOTE: This story was supported by Journalismfund Europe.
__
Made up of more than 40 small islands, the Guaitecas Archipelago is a gateway to Chile’s Patagonia region that is one of the world’s most remote places. Despite being a national reserve, it’s also home to numerous salmon farms that discharge hundreds of tons of chemicals and antibiotics into the sea every year.
At least 313 salmon farms were authorized in the archipelago, according to Terram, a Chilean foundation focused on sustainable development.
Leviñanco and Vera Perez say the intensive farming damaged where they fished, so they decided to try to counter that. They started bringing in healthy mussels and clams from other areas. Friends and family thought they were crazy, but over years the work paid off.
“The fish, birds and other marine animals came back,” said Leviñanco.
